newsitem.title: USA: US AIRWAYS PILOTS MAKE COUNTER-OFFER TO FIRM.
newsitem.headline: US AIRWAYS PILOTS MAKE COUNTER-OFFER TO FIRM.

text.p: In an effort to reach a labor agreement with US Airways Group Inc, its pilots union said it submitted a new contract proposal that gives ground on one controversial issue, but holds steady on others.
In the latest offer, the union increased its offer on a key issue about the development of a low-cost unit to compete with rivals such as Southwest Airlines Co and Delta Air Lines Inc's Express unit.
The airline and the pilots union previously said that a low-cost unit needs to be developed to defend against the growing threat of regional and low-cost carriers.
The two sides, however, disagree on the size and scope of the unit.
US Airways sought to have the low-cost unit handle about 30 to 40 percent of its flights, the union said.
The pilots, however, said since the airline only faces competition from low-cost carriers on 5.5 percent of its flights, the unit should comprise only 10 percent of US Airways' operations.
Now, the pilots' latest proposal increases the proposed size of the unit, said Mike Oakey, a spokesman for the pilots. The union declined to outline specifics.
While the Air Line Pilots Association moved towards a compromise on the low-cost unit, it made other demands about the company's future growth.

The company recently said it would commit to expansion, instead of shrinking the airline as it had done over the past six years. US Airways proposed using the airline's size in June 1998 as the "baseline" level upon which any future growth would be based. The union's new proposal, however, calls for June 1997 to be the baseline for any expansion.
The union also seeks the return of furloughed pilots.

US Airways, the nation's sixth largest airline, has been in contract talks with its pilots since their contract became amendable in April 1996. The airline, which has among the highest costs in the industry, said it will be forced to downsize unless it reaches a cost-cutting pact with its unionized workers.
US Airways has received the pilots' latest proposal but has not yet responded.
